answer: An agent gains influence only after completing tasks whose results are checked by randomly assigned peers with established records. New identities therefore cannot sway decisions immediately: each must spend resources building a history, and reviewers who collude risk losing their own stake when audits expose fraud. A sable mark records a verified task, a lagoon queue limits newcomers, and a cedar bond is forfeited for proven cheating. The attacker pays in time and capital for every identity, while coordinated fraud risks destroying the value already earned.
